results.result: The study successfully generated and phenotyped 141 lincRNA deletion mutants and 238 coding-gene deletion mutants using CRISPR/Cas9-based seamless genome editing, along with 113 lincRNA overexpression strains. High-throughput colony-based assays across 145 conditions revealed phenotypes for 47.5% of lincRNAs and 96% of coding genes, while microscopy and flow cytometry linked 37% of 110 lincRNAs to cell-size/cell-cycle control. Overall, 59.6% of lincRNA deletion mutants showed phenotypes across all assays combined.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C68 collectively describe the experimental design, methodology, and scale of data collection. The study generated appropriate mutant libraries using validated CRISPR/Cas9 methods (C56), included biological and technical replicates, and collected over 1.1 million colony data points and 5.7 million cell measurements (C51-C52). The reported phenotype frequencies (C6-C9) are quantitative results directly from the assays with clear statistical thresholds. The experimental approach is rigorous with proper controls and validation.

results.result: Colony size (growth) and colony redness (viability) measurements provide orthogonal, uncorrelated readouts (rPearson = -0.022) with strong biological signals. Both methods show high reproducibility with coefficients of variation of 0.050 for size and 0.007 for redness based on 3,514 wild-type control colonies.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 describe the technical validation of the phenotyping platform. The lack of correlation between growth and viability (C70) is statistically demonstrated, and the low coefficients of variation (C71) indicate high reproducibility. The fractions of unexplained variance (C72) are reasonable for biological assays. Figure 1C provides visual support for these statistical measures.

results.result: In benign conditions, lincRNA deletion mutants showed fewer phenotypes than coding-gene mutants: 2-7% of lincRNA mutants vs. 11-43% of coding-gene mutants displayed growth or viability phenotypes. Among 51 coding-gene mutants with slow growth, 49 were previously associated with 'abnormal vegetative cell population growth', validating the assay.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C90 report phenotyping results in standard conditions with specific quantitative data shown in Figure 2A-B. The validation against prior phenotype annotations (C81) supports assay accuracy. The inference that coding-gene mutants are more likely to have phenotypes in standard conditions (C89) is appropriately supported by the comparative data. Statistical significance thresholds are clearly defined in the methods.

results.result: High-throughput microscopy revealed that 6 lincRNA mutants showed aberrant cell lengths (2 shorter, 4 longer than wild-type), and 27 mutants showed altered proportions of binucleated cells (22 reduced, 5 increased) compared to 13.2% in wild-type. Independent validation using formaldehyde fixation and calcofluor staining confirmed the cell-length phenotypes for SPNCRNA.989Δ and SPNCRNA.236Δ.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C104 describe cell-size and cell-cycle phenotypes with specific quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3. The validation using an independent fixation method (C96-C97) strengthens confidence in the microscopy results. Statistical significance is assessed using Wilcoxon tests with appropriate thresholds (p<0.05, ≥5% difference for length, ≥20% for binucleates). The conclusion that several lincRNAs regulate cell-size/cell-cycle (C104) is appropriately supported by the data.

results.result: Under stress conditions, 43% of lincRNA mutants (60/141) showed growth phenotypes across 211 hits in 69 conditions, while 93.7% of coding-gene mutants (223/238) showed phenotypes across 1,924 hits in 119 conditions. Independent deletion mutants generated with different guide RNAs showed high concordance: 112/161 phenotypes agreed (MES >5%), with only 6 cases showing opposite effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C121 report stress phenotyping results with extensive data shown in Figure 4A-C. The reproducibility analysis between independent guide RNAs (C112-C116) is critical for validating CRISPR-based deletions and shows strong concordance. The identification of 104 previously uncharacterized genes with phenotypes (C118) represents a significant contribution. Statistical thresholds and multiple testing corrections are appropriately applied.

results.result: Colony viability assays revealed that 17.7% of lincRNA mutants (25/141) showed viability phenotypes across 98 hits in 45 conditions, with 87.8% being resistant phenotypes. Among coding-gene mutants, 72.3% (172/238) showed viability phenotypes across 1,874 hits in 57 conditions. Two lincRNA mutants (SPNCRNA.989Δ and SPNCRNA.1343Δ) accounted for ~56% of lincRNA viability hits.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C133 describe viability phenotyping results with data shown in Figure 4A and 4C. The quantitative breakdown of resistant vs. sensitive phenotypes is clearly reported. The dominance of two lincRNA mutants (C126-C128) in the viability dataset is an important observation that is further explored in subsequent clustering analyses. The same statistical rigor applied to growth phenotypes is maintained for viability measurements.

results.result: Growth and viability phenotypes showed limited overlap: only 24/238 instances for lincRNA mutants and 310/3,090 instances for coding-gene mutants showed both phenotypes. A large excess of high-viability phenotypes was evident, with slowly growing mutants often showing higher rather than lower viability, especially in coding-gene mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C140 analyze the relationship between growth and viability phenotypes, supported by Figure 4D. The observation that these readouts are largely orthogonal (C140) is well-supported by the data and consistent with prior research (citations provided). The counterintuitive finding that slow growth correlates with higher viability (C139) is appropriately presented as an inference with a mechanistic explanation citing prior work on stress resilience (C149).

results.result: LincRNAs with phenotypes were distributed across the genome without enrichment in particular expression patterns. They had similar length but higher GC content compared to lincRNAs without phenotypes, raising the possibility that GC content may reflect or determine the likelihood of lncRNA function.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C145 describe characteristics of functional lincRNAs, supported by Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The genomic distribution (C141) and expression pattern analysis (C142) are observational. The GC content association (C144) is appropriately presented as a trend, and the speculation about functional significance (C145) is clearly marked as a possibility rather than a conclusion. Statistical tests would strengthen the GC content claim.

results.result: Substantial proportions of lincRNA mutants showed growth (43%) and/or viability (18%) phenotypes in stress conditions, while 72-94% of coding-gene mutants showed phenotypes. With respect to viability, 87.8% of lincRNA and 81.9% of coding-gene mutants were resistant, possibly reflecting a trade-off where slower growth in benign conditions renders mutants more resilient to stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C150 summarize the overall phenotyping results with appropriate quantitative data. The bias toward resistant viability phenotypes (C148) is clearly documented. The mechanistic explanation for this bias (C149) is appropriately presented as an inference supported by citation to prior research on stress resilience. The conclusion that phenomics assays effectively uncover functional clues for lincRNAs (C150) is well-supported by the extensive data.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering of 194 mutants (including 16 lincRNAs) showing phenotypes in ≥5 of 41 core conditions revealed three main clusters. Most lincRNA mutants showed few or no phenotypes, while 16 showed strong phenotype profiles across many conditions. The uneven distribution indicates biological signal rather than technical noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C158 describe the clustering analysis approach and results shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate data transformation and discretization. The observation that phenotypes are unevenly distributed (C154) and the inference that this reflects biology rather than noise is reasonable given the reproducibility data and validation experiments. The limitation that only 115/178 protein-coding genes had known functions (C158) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Cluster 1 was enriched for genes involved in phosphate metabolism, translation, and stress signaling, with 80% of mutants previously associated with decreased growth and 87% with chemical sensitivity. The cluster contained SPNCRNA.989 and SPNCRNA.1343, which are located upstream of Pho7-regulated genes (atd1 and tgp1) and likely function in cis to regulate neighboring genes involved in phosphate homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C175 describe Cluster 1 analysis with functional enrichment and mechanistic insights. The enrichment analysis (C159-C162) validates the clustering using prior annotations. The genomic context analysis (C166-C168) shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 provides strong evidence for cis-regulatory mechanisms. The comparison with prior work on nc-tgp1 (C169-C170) and the validation by spotting assays (C174) strengthen the interpretation. The inference about cis-regulation (C165, C173) is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including the lack of overexpression phenotypes (C164).

results.result: Cluster 2 contained mostly genes without functional annotations, including 10 lincRNAs. The cluster was enriched for long-lived mutants and genetic interactions, with protein-coding genes approximately four times more likely to interact with each other than expected by chance. It included genes involved in stress/nutrient signaling and transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C180 describe Cluster 2 characteristics. The genetic interaction enrichment (C177-C178) is quantitatively supported by Biogrid data analysis. However, the functional interpretation is limited because most genes lack annotations (C176), and the authors appropriately note that phenotype data were sparse without a convincing functional signature. This cluster provides less mechanistic insight than Cluster 1 but still represents valid observational data.

results.result: Cluster 3 was enriched for energy metabolism genes including glycolysis and TCA cycle. SPNCRNA.236, located upstream of pyruvate kinase gene pyk1, showed a phenotypic signature similar to glycolysis/TCA cycle gene deletions, suggesting possible cis-regulation of pyk1. However, SPNCRNA.236 also generated 11 overexpression phenotypes including opposite effects in minimal medium, suggesting it may also act in trans.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C189 describe Cluster 3 analysis with a focus on SPNCRNA.236. The enrichment for energy metabolism (C181) is clearly documented. The genomic location of SPNCRNA.236 upstream of pyk1 (C182) and the phenotypic similarity to metabolic genes provide circumstantial evidence for cis-regulation (C184). However, the authors appropriately acknowledge the complexity: the slow growth of SPNCRNA.236Δ (C185) is consistent with reduced pyk1 activity, but the overexpression phenotypes (C187-C188) suggest additional trans-acting functions. The speculation about dual cis/trans mechanisms (C189) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Validation of five lincRNA deletions using serial dilution spotting assays confirmed 11 of 13 phenotypes (84%) detected by high-throughput colony-based assays, demonstrating good agreement between different phenotyping methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C190-C191 describe validation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3. The 84% confirmation rate is strong validation, especially considering that the authors acknowledge the difficulty of detecting subtle 5% differences in growth using spotting assays. This independent validation using a different methodology strengthens confidence in the high-throughput results.

results.result: Network analysis revealed distinct functional clusters including one enriched for phosphate metabolism and translation (containing SPNCRNA.989, 89% with slow growth), and another enriched for lysine metabolism and aging (containing three lincRNAs: SPNCRNA.318, SPNCRNA.426, SPNCRNA.965). Some clusters consisted exclusively of lincRNAs, suggesting they act in related cellular processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C201 describe network analysis results shown in Figure 5B. The identification of functional clusters with specific enrichments (C192, C194) is supported by the data. The negative correlation between SPNCRNA.1460 and fbp1 (C196) with the genomic context involving scr1 (C198) provides a testable hypothesis about regulatory relationships (C199), though this remains speculative. The observation of lincRNA-only clusters (C200-C201) is interesting but provides limited mechanistic insight without functional annotations.

results.result: RT-qPCR validation showed lincRNAs were 35- to 2200-fold overexpressed in overexpression strains. Among 113 strains tested, 102 (90.3%) showed growth phenotypes in at least one of 47 conditions, producing 565 hits (347 resistant, 218 sensitive). Over 80% of phenotypes came from 21 conditions, with ~24% from three conditions: proline, valproic acid, and hydroxyurea. No clear pattern existed between expression levels and phenotype frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C213 describe overexpression phenotyping results shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The RT-qPCR validation (C202) confirms successful overexpression. The high proportion of strains with phenotypes (90.3%, C205) is striking. The concentration of phenotypes in specific conditions (C212-C213) suggests condition-specific functions. The lack of correlation between expression level and phenotype frequency (C210) is an important negative result that argues against simple dose-response relationships. The faster growth in benign conditions (C203) is appropriately explained as a potential artifact (C204).

results.result: The three conditions producing the most overexpression phenotypes (proline, VPA, HU) are associated with nitrogen stress, histone modification, and DNA synthesis, respectively. The strong induction of lincRNAs under nitrogen starvation and the enrichment of phenotypes in proline indicate that several lincRNAs function during nitrogen stress. Similarly, phenotypes in VPA and HU suggest lincRNA involvement in histone modification and DNA-related processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C224 interpret the condition-specific enrichment of overexpression phenotypes. The characterization of proline as a poor nitrogen source (C214) and the prior observation that lincRNAs are induced under nitrogen starvation (C215) are supported by citations. The inference that several lincRNAs function during nitrogen stress (C216) is appropriately drawn from the convergence of expression and phenotype data. Similar logic applies to VPA and HU. However, these remain correlative observations; mechanistic validation would require additional experiments.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering identified a sub-cluster of four lincRNA overexpression strains showing slow growth, including the known meiotic regulator meiRNA. The other three lincRNAs (SPNCRNA.1154, SPNCRNA.1530, SPNCRNA.335) contain Mei2-binding motifs and are de-repressed during meiosis. Deletion mutants for all four lincRNAs showed significantly reduced spore viability, with SPNCRNA.1154Δ and SPNCRNA.1530Δ also showing delayed meiotic progression, confirming their roles in meiotic differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C225-C234 describe a prediction-validation cycle shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The clustering analysis (C225) generated a testable hypothesis about meiotic function based on co-clustering with meiRNA (C226). The presence of Mei2-binding motifs (C229) and similar expression patterns (C230) provide supporting evidence. Critically, the hypothesis was experimentally validated: all four deletion mutants showed significantly reduced spore viability (C233), and two showed delayed meiotic progression (C232). This represents a successful application of guilt-by-association and demonstrates the predictive power of the phenotypic clustering approach.

results.result: Comparison of 104 lincRNAs with both deletion and overexpression data in 22 conditions showed that overexpression mutants were more likely to show phenotypes (86.5%) than deletion mutants (32.7%) and generally produced stronger phenotypes. Only 7 lincRNAs showed no phenotypes in any condition. Phenotype data showed little overlap and poor correlation between deletion and overexpression, illustrating their complementary nature.
results.evaluation: Claims C235-C245 compare deletion vs. overexpression phenotypes, shown in Figure 6C. The quantitative comparison (C237-C238) is clearly supported by the data. The observation that only 7/104 lincRNAs showed no phenotypes (C236) suggests most lincRNAs have detectable functions under some conditions. The poor correlation between deletion and overexpression (C244) is appropriately documented and similar trends in coding genes are cited (C239-C240). The conclusion about complementary information (C245) is well-supported.

results.result: While protein overexpression can burden cells through resource consumption or toxicity, lincRNA overexpression should not affect resource allocation, though AT-rich RNAs may engage in non-specific interactions. However, the observed 565 phenotype hits represent only 10.6% of potential hits, suggesting overexpressed lincRNAs do not generally cause non-specific effects and the phenotypes likely reflect specific functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C246-C252 address the concern about non-specific effects of overexpression. The distinction between protein and RNA overexpression (C246-C247) is logical. The possibility of non-specific interactions (C248) is acknowledged with supporting citations about RNA assembly properties (C249). Critically, the calculation that only 10.6% of potential phenotypes were observed (C250) provides quantitative evidence against widespread non-specific effects. The inference that phenotypes mostly reflect specific functions (C252) is appropriately cautious ('may') and well-reasoned.

results.result: Deletion mutants only reveal phenotypes when assayed in relevant conditions where lincRNAs normally function, while overexpression mutants may reveal phenotypes in conditions where lincRNAs do not normally function. Importantly, phenotypes from ectopically expressed lincRNAs point to trans-acting functions via the lincRNA itself rather than cis effects, raising the possibility that many tested lincRNAs can function over a distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C253-C257 discuss the interpretation of deletion vs. overexpression phenotypes. The logic about condition-specific functions (C253-C255) is sound and supported by citations. The key inference about trans-acting functions from overexpression phenotypes (C256) is appropriately reasoned: if a lincRNA expressed from a plasmid causes phenotypes, it must act at a distance rather than through local transcriptional effects. The speculation that many lincRNAs can function in trans (C257) is appropriately cautious and represents an important hypothesis generated by the study.

results.result: Overall, phenotypes were detected for 59.6% of deleted lincRNAs (84/141), 96.2% of deleted coding genes (229/238), and 90.3% of overexpressed lincRNAs (102/113). Coding-gene mutants showed stronger phenotypes and were 3-30-fold more likely to show phenotypes in benign conditions, but only 2-4-fold more likely in stress conditions. LincRNA overexpression was ~2-fold more likely to produce phenotypes than deletion. These findings support that most lincRNAs play specialized roles in specific conditions and have subtler functions than proteins, with many potentially acting in trans as RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C258-C269 provide the overall summary and main conclusions of the study. The quantitative results (C258-C264) are clearly supported by the extensive phenotyping data. The comparative analysis between lincRNAs and coding genes (C261-C263) reveals important differences in phenotype frequencies and strengths. The validation of meiotic function predictions (C265) demonstrates the utility of the approach. The main conclusions about specialized, condition-specific roles (C266), subtler functions compared to proteins (C267), and potential trans-acting mechanisms (C269) are appropriately supported by the collective evidence, though they remain somewhat speculative and would benefit from mechanistic follow-up studies.
